title: Brick by BRICS: Where countries in conflict seek common ground
text:
Brick by BRICS: Where countries in conflict seek common ground
As developing and emerging-market countries met for their annual summit in India, they and other alliances are looking to counter Donald Trump’s worldview.
Chinese President Xi Jinping stood beside Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi over the weekend, six years after troops from their respective countries fought a deadly clash along the disputed Himalayan border.
The setting was the BRICS summit – an annual meeting of developing nations and emerging economies, set up in 2009 as a counterpoint to the West.
While there are certainly tensions between some of the 11 full members, President Xi’s first visit to India in seven years demonstrated that they are united in one thing: a desire for their countries to have a greater say in the world order, especially in the current political climate.
The leaders of some of the world’s major emerging economies met for the annual BRICS summit in New Delhi. They and other alliances are looking to counter President Donald Trump’s worldview.
Today, it’s the actions of U.S. President Donald Trump that are giving the bloc fresh impetus, say experts.
“So much of what has galvanized the BRICS members and aspiring BRICS members [are] the policies of the Trump administration,” says Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council.
That appears to be part of a wider trend around the globe. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says his country is seeking a “unique alliance” with the European Union as its trade war with the U.S. continues. He will address the EU in Strasbourg later this week.
And in the Middle East, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed a defense and security alliance last month amid the ongoing U.S.-Iran war.
Not a unified anti-Western bloc
But, in the case of BRICS, that discontent has not created a unified anti-Western bloc.
China and India weren’t the only nations in attendance hoping to overcome differences. At the same summit, Iran’s president met the crown prince of Abu Dhabi. The two have been on opposite sides in the current Middle East war, with Iran launching drone attacks against the United Arab Emirates because of its close ties to the United States and Israel.
In the end, they backed the BRICS call for restraint, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian saying they had agreed to “put the past aside and look forward to the future.”
Commentators believe that, despite such tensions, members of BRICS believe it still has an important role to play in helping their nations.
“BRICS is a very heterogeneous institution,” says Rajan Kumar, a professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University’s School of International Relations in Delhi. Its members differ in history, political systems, and geography, he says, yet their repeated meetings show that they “take this forum very seriously.”
The first summit involved just four countries, initially named BRIC after founding members Brazil, Russia, India, and China. South Africa joined the following year, creating BRICS, and now Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE are included among its ranks.
Together, they account for about half the world’s population, 40% of global gross domestic product, and 26% of global trade.
“Behave like an equal”
The rise of BRICS also comes amid growing frustration in the developing world that institutions such as the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and the U.N. Security Council no longer reflect the economic and political weight of countries in the Global South – a collective term for developing and middle-income countries.
“We’ve seen in recent years increasing levels of concern, particularly in the Global South, about the direction of global affairs,” says Mr. Kugelman. “That includes the major wars that have been playing out, but also the policies of the West, particularly when it comes to the global economy.”
But, he adds, “There is no clarity within the membership on what BRICS is truly all about. ... How is it meant to position itself relative to the West?”
The question is especially consequential when it comes to attempts to reduce reliance on the U.S. dollar, with members divided over how far BRICS should go in challenging Western financial systems.
While Russia and Iran have pushed more strongly for reducing dependence on Western financial systems, India and most other BRICS members have sought greater room to maneuver, without taking a hostile position toward the U.S. and Europe.
Trade between BRICS members, though, has increased dramatically from about $84 billion in 2003 to $1.17 trillion in 2024, according to India’s Commerce Ministry.
And the growing number of countries seeking BRICS membership would suggest that many do see it as relevant.
For Professor Kumar, part of BRICS’ attraction is that underrepresented countries can “behave like an equal.”
The differences were visible in New Delhi, but the members nevertheless signed a joint declaration covering trade, finance, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, and global conflicts.
Mr. Kugelman says the contradictions are unlikely to disappear, but economic pressures confronting many countries in the Global South are likely to keep BRICS viable.
“So long as the global economy is in a rough place,” he says, “that will be motivation for BRICS.”
